question: The NIA Intervention Testing Program found that rapamycin lengthens life in both sexes of mice. What is true of the other anti-ageing interventions it identified?
answers: They are sex specific: they extend lifespan in one sex but have little or no effect on the other

receipt.quote: Second, rapamycin increases the lifespan of both male and female mice, which is unique because of all of the other anti-aging interventions identified by the NIA Intervention Testing Program are sex specific, i.e., they significantly increased lifespan in one sex but have little or no effect on the other sex [18].

question: What made the 2009 mouse study of rapamycin feeding surprising in terms of when the drug was started?
answers: Rapamycin extended lifespan even when given late in life (19 months of age)
It worked when started late, not only early in life

receipt.quote: The study was initiated in 2006, and in 2009, Harrison et al. [6] reported the first data showing that feeding rapamycin (14 ppm or ~ 2.24 mg/kg based on average food consumption of mice) increased the lifespan of both male and female mice. Not only was this the first report to show that lifespan could be increased pharmacologically in both male and female mice, but more importantly, the increase in lifespan was observed when rapamycin was given to mice late in life (19 months).

question: In mice, how did the lifespan benefit of rapamycin compare when treatment started at 4, 9 or 19 months of age?
answers: The increase in lifespan was similar at all three start ages
Starting late gave a similar benefit to starting early

receipt.quote: Interestingly, the increase in lifespan by rapamycin was similar when implemented at 4 months [16], 9 months [17], or 19 months [6] of age.

question: Why is the effect of rapamycin on mouse lifespan described as robust?
answers: It has been replicated in many laboratories, in different mouse strains (from inbred to the heterogeneous UM-HET3) and with different dosing regimens

receipt.quote: As shown in Table 1, the effect of rapamycin on lifespan is robust because it has been replicated in many different laboratories with different strains of laboratory mice, ranging from inbred strains (e.g., C57BL/6 and 129) to the UM-HET3 mice (a heterogeneous strain of mice generated by a 4-way cross) and with different rapamycin dosing regimens.
